title: Nvidia vs Coca-Cola
intro: Arora's paradox: the faster grower at the lower multiple lost the year. Why that's not a market error.

steps.title: The paradox
steps.body:
Nvidia: earnings growing **60–70%**, at a **lower P/E than Coca-Cola**. Coke: growing **6–7%**.

'Ideally, that should not happen' — a much faster grower at a cheaper multiple should be the obvious buy. And yet **Coca-Cola outperformed Nvidia this year**. Arora's blunt line: *this is not how markets work.*

steps.title: The three questions
steps.body:
Headline growth rates answer none of the questions that matter:

1. **What kind** of growth is it — franchise expansion, cyclical windfall, capex surge?
2. **How durable** is it — does the sector attract capital and competition that mean-revert the rate?
3. **How much is already priced in** — a multiple is a forecast, not a discount coupon.

steps.title: The two profiles
steps.body: Coke's growth is slower but **steadier and easier to predict** — predictability itself earns a premium. Nvidia's growth is real but sits inside a **hot, competitive, capital-attracting cycle** — the market keeps re-pricing its durability.

points.label: Rate
points.note: The headline number — the least informative of the three.

points.label: Durability
points.note: The market's real question: will year three look like year one? Hot cycles say maybe not — hence the 'cheap' multiple.

points.label: Predictability
points.note: Coke's 6–7% arrives on schedule. Scheduled growth compounds plans as well as capital.

steps.title: Reading the anomaly
steps.body: > [!warn] A screen flagging 'high growth + low P/E' as a bargain often collects businesses whose growth the market has correctly diagnosed as perishable. **The anomaly is the message** — investigate it, don't pocket it.

recap:
**Growth has a kind, a durability, and a price already paid.**

- Faster + cheaper lost to slower + steadier this year — by design, not error.
- The multiple encodes the market's durability judgement.
- Predictable growth earns its premium.
- Treat too-cheap fast growers as questions, not gifts.
